newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavaria deal seals fate of unpopular sick pay cuts.
newsitem.headline: Bavaria deal seals fate of unpopular sick pay cuts.

text.p: The German engineering industry on Thursday struck another big regional wage accord guaranteeing full pay during sickness, sealing the fate of plans to implement an unpopular law allowing sick pay cuts.
Metal and engineering employers in the southern state of Bavaria said they reached a wage deal with the IG Metall trade union there, averting strikes threatened in the region.

The deal, which covers 650,000 workers, means the majority of Germany's 3.2 million engineering workers have succeeded in avoiding a 20 percent sick pay cut which they have bitterly opposed in demonstrations and walkouts.
The law, which came into force last October, was originially seen as a gift from Chancellor Helmut Kohl to employers who have long bemoaned Germany's high labour costs.

The Bavaria deal set pay rises of 1.5 percent from April 1 next year and 2.5 percent from April 1998, similar to accords reached on Wednesday in the sector's largest region, North Rhine-Westphalia, which has 850,000 workers, and in the southern part of the state of Baden-Wuerrtemberg.

Engineering employers have had to accept that, given the extent of worker resistance to the cuts, they will not be able to attain in 1997 the sweeping labour cost reductions they had initially been hoping for.

Hundreds of thousands of workers have staged walkouts in recent months in defence of full sick pay, determined not to give up a privilege which an earlier generation fought for and won in strikes during the 1950s.
"The government and employers totally miscalculated the situation and fell flat on their faces," said IG Metall spokeswoman Nele Loew Beer.
Talks with employers had been deadlocked until a breakthrough was reached last Thursday in the northern state of Lower Saxony, offering workers continued full sick pay and modest wage gains.
Rainer Hildmann, chief negotiator for the Bavarian employers, told journalists the Bavarian package "was not a good agreement" with terms largely dictated by those of the Lower Saxony accord.
IG Metall Bavaria chief Werner Neugebauer called it an acceptable compromise.
Like other regional deals, the Bavaria agreement cuts the Christmas bonus to 55 percent from 60 percent of pay. Also, overtime payments will no longer be taken into account when calculating sick pay.
Further talks have been set in other regions. IG Metall said talks covering more than 400,000 workers in the states of Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland are scheduled for December 18.
Talks will also be held for the northern part of the state of Baden-Wuerrtemberg and for the coastal region covering Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburg, Bremen and the northwestern part of Lower Saxony.
